blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Variational methods estimate the optical flow between two frames by minimizing an energy that combines
a data term, derived from brightness constancy, with a regularizer weighted by a parameter α > 0 \alpha>0 . The
quality of the estimate depends strongly on α \alpha . Too small a value leaves the flow noisy, and too
large a value oversmooths it. This paper studies the choice of α \alpha by bilevel learning from
ground-truth flow and asks, in a fully discrete setting, when an optimal parameter exists and when it is
positive.

blocks.en:
The linearized brightness constancy
constraint gives one equation per pixel for the two flow components, so the flow is not determined
locally (the aperture problem). Lucas and Kanade Lucas and Kanade (1981) assume that the flow is constant
in a window around each pixel and solve the resulting local least-squares problems. Horn and
Schunck Horn and Schunck (1981) instead add a global quadratic penalty on the flow gradient, which
yields dense flow fields but smooths motion boundaries. Total variation (TV)
regularization, introduced for image denoising Rudin et al. (1992) , preserves such boundaries.
Shulman and Hervé Shulman and
Hervé (1989) proposed an early non-quadratic regularizer for
discontinuous flow fields, and TV is widely used for optical
flow Rouchouze et al. (1994) ; Deriche et al. (1996) ; Zach et al. (2007) ; Wedel et al. (2009) ; Chambolle and
Pock (2011) ; Ranftl et al. (2014) ; Ali et al. (2016) .
We use its isotropic form, applied to each flow component. TV is convex but not differentiable, and it is
usually minimized by primal–dual methods Chambolle (2004) ; Zach et al. (2007) ; Chambolle and
Pock (2011) or
replaced by a smooth approximation such as the Huber function Kalmoun (2018) . The combined
local-global (CLG) model of Bruhn et al. Bruhn et al. (2005) joins the Lucas–Kanade data term with a global
regularizer. It inherits the robustness of the local method and the density of the global one, and it
can be minimized efficiently, for instance by multigrid methods Kalmoun and Garrido (2013) . Spatially varying
parameters α ⁡ ( p ) \alpha(p) adapted to image features have also been
proposed Wedel et al. (2009) ; Belhachmi and Hecht (2011) ; Belhachmi and Hecht (2016) .

blocks.en:
Problem ( 1.1 ) rests on four modeling choices. First, the parameter is learned from
ground truth. Classical parameter-choice rules, such as the discrepancy
principle Engl et al. (1996) , the L-curve Hansen (1992) , generalized
cross-validation Golub et al. (1979) and Stein’s unbiased risk estimate Stein (1981) , need no ground
truth. They rely instead on knowledge of the noise or on heuristic criteria, and they do not target the
flow error itself. Bilevel learning uses training data with known ground truth and minimizes the
reconstruction error directly. Second, the upper-level loss is the squared
Euclidean distance, which equals the sum over all pixels of the squared endpoint errors, a standard
accuracy measure for optical flow Baker et al. (2011) . It is smooth in w w , whereas the endpoint error
itself and the angular error Barron et al. (1994) are not differentiable where the error vanishes.
Third, a single scalar parameter is the natural first case. It is the setting in which existence and
positivity can be characterized by explicit conditions, and spatially varying parameters, as in the
bilevel framework of Pagliari et al. (2022) , can build on it. Fourth, the CLG data term makes the
lower-level problem well posed. When every window contains two pixels with linearly independent
gradients, the data term is strongly convex, and the lower-level solution is unique for every α ≥ 0 \alpha\geq 0 , including α = 0 \alpha=0 (Lemma 1 ). The Horn–Schunck data term alone is never
strongly convex, because its matrix J ⊤ ​ J J^{\top}J in ( 2.1 ) has a null space of dimension at least N N .

blocks.en:
Bilevel learning of regularization parameters in imaging was established by Kunisch and
Pock Kunisch and Pock (2013) for variational denoising and by De los Reyes and
Schönlieb De los Reyes and
Schönlieb (2013) for learning noise models in TV denoising. Its theory
includes existence results for a broad class of regularizers De los Reyes
et al. (2016) , refined
stationarity systems for TV De los Reyes and
Villacís (2022) , stationarity and second-order conditions through
a reformulation as a mathematical program with complementarity constraints De los Reyes (2023) , and
spatially dependent parameters Pagliari et al. (2022) . For finite-dimensional linear inverse problems
with a continuously differentiable regularizer, Ehrhardt, Gazzola and Scott Ehrhardt et al. (2025) give
a sufficient condition for a positive optimal parameter. Our positivity result for the quadratic model
(Theorem 3 ) is a special case of their condition. Applications include blind
deconvolution Hintermüller and
Wu (2015) and the learning of fractional differential
operators Bartels and
Weber (2023) , and Crockett and Fessler Crockett and
Fessler (2022) survey the field.
Computational work addresses inexact lower-level solves through derivative-free
methods Ehrhardt and
Roberts (2021) , inexact hypergradients Ehrhardt and
Roberts (2024) and single-loop
schemes Suonperä and
Valkonen (2025) . Learning through truncated or approximate
inference Domke (2012) ; Domke (2013) and learned variational inference layers Ranftl and Pock (2014) aim at empirical performance rather than at the analysis of a regularization weight. For optical flow,
Jiang et al. Jiang et al. (2020) use a bilevel scheme that couples flow and camera motion in unsupervised
deep learning. Closest to the present setting, El Hakoume et al. El Hakoume et al. (2023) learn the two
Lamé coefficients of a fluid optical flow registration model by bilevel supervised learning, within a
multi-frame super-resolution method. Positivity is imposed through a fixed box, uniqueness of the
lower-level solution is assumed, and the bilevel problem “is not theoretically studied” because their
model lacks the required regularity. Related work by Laghrib and coauthors learns spatially varying weights
for nonlocal deblurring El Malki et al. (2024) . To our knowledge, no previous work establishes existence,
positivity and second-order conditions for learning the regularization parameter of a variational
optical flow model from ground-truth flow. Here all
objects are finite-dimensional, the proofs are direct, and the conditions are explicit and computable from
the data for both regularizers.

blocks.en:
The main contributions are the following. • A finite-dimensional bilevel formulation for CLG optical flow in which a scalar regularization
parameter is learned from ground-truth flow. • Existence of an optimal parameter. For any convex regularizer that vanishes only at zero, a
sufficient condition is that the Lucas–Kanade estimate be closer to the ground truth than the zero
flow (Proposition 2 ). For TV with zero boundary values this condition is not needed,
because the lower-level solution vanishes beyond a finite value of α \alpha (Corollary 5 ). • Sufficient conditions under which α = 0 \alpha=0 is not optimal, so that every optimal parameter is
positive, for the quadratic model
(Theorem 3 , an instance of the condition of Ehrhardt et al. (2025) ) and for TV
(Theorem 8 ), and second-order sufficient conditions for strict local optimality in the
quadratic model (Theorem 4 ). The TV condition is not covered by Ehrhardt et al. (2025) ,
because TV is not differentiable, and it differs structurally from the analyses of scalar data
terms De los Reyes
et al. (2016) ; De los Reyes and
Villacís (2022) .
The Lucas–Kanade data term couples the two flow components through 2 × 2 2\times 2 blocks that vary from
pixel to pixel. This coupling requires a four-way partition of the pixels, a term ℛ mix \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{mix}} for the pixels at which only one flow component has a nonzero gradient, and a
term ℛ var \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{var}} for the spatial variation of the blocks. These terms vanish for spatially
uniform scalar data terms. • Synthetic examples that illustrate the conditions, including cases in which the sufficient
conditions fail.

blocks.en: 2 Discrete Setting and Problem Formulation
blocks.zh: 2 设置和问题的制定

blocks.en:
All objects in this paper are finite-dimensional. The image domain Ω \Omega is a rectangular grid of N = n y ​ n x N=n_{y}n_{x} pixels with unit grid spacing, ordered row by row. Scalar fields on Ω \Omega , such as images,

5 Illustrative Examples
blocks.zh: 5 示例

blocks.en: We present numerical examples that illustrate the theoretical conditions, including cases in which the sufficient conditions fail. These examples are not intended as a performance evaluation or comparison with state-of-the-art methods. Two scales are considered: a 3 × 3 3\times 3 grid (and a 4 × 4 4\times 4 grid in Example 6 ), which allows direct inspection of all conditions, and a 50 × 50 50\times 50 grid, which exercises the framework at a more realistic scale with noise and subpixel motion.

blocks.en:
The results of this paper hold under assumptions that restrict their scope, and some of the conditions
are conservative. We summarize these restrictions below.

A single scalar parameter is learned from one pair of frames with an exact ground-truth flow. We do not

suitable for other pairs. The examples are small synthetic scenes chosen to illustrate the conditions,
